title: Media and Digital Citizenship
summary: Types and roles of media, bias and fake news, evaluating sources, online safety and privacy, digital footprints, cyberbullying, and responsible social media use.

notes.text: The **media** are ways of communicating information to many people: newspapers, radio, television, websites, podcasts and **social media** (such as TikTok, Instagram, WhatsApp and YouTube).

items: **Hold leaders accountable** by exposing corruption (the 'watchdog' role).

notes.text: Presenting information in a one-sided way, favouring one view over others.
False or misleading information presented as news. **Misinformation** is shared by mistake; **disinformation** is spread on purpose to deceive.

notes.caption: How to check a source
rows: Who wrote it and who published it?
Is it a reliable, known organisation or an anonymous account?
Old stories are often reshared as if they were new
Are sources, data or experts named?
Do other reliable sources report the same thing?
Check at least two trusted sources
Is it designed to make me angry or afraid?
Could the image be edited or AI-generated?

notes.title: Checking a viral post
notes.problem: A post says, 'Share now! Schools close tomorrow!' with no source. How do you check it?
steps: Check the date and whether other reliable sites report it.
Be suspicious of urgent demands to share.
notes.answer: Check the Department of Education or your school before believing it.

items: Never share passwords, your home address, ID number or bank details.
Use strong passwords and two-step verification.
Set social media accounts to **private** and accept only people you know.
Never meet someone you only know online without a trusted adult.
Be careful of **scams** (messages promising prizes or asking for money) and **grooming** (adults pretending to be young to gain a child's trust).
Think before sharing images: once something is online you lose control of it.

notes.text: The permanent record of everything you do online: posts, photos, comments, likes and searches. Future employers and universities may look at it.

notes.title: Safe or unsafe?
notes.problem: A new online 'friend' asks for your address and a photo. What should you do?
steps: Never share personal details with strangers.
notes.answer: Do not reply; block, report and tell an adult.

notes.text: Cyberbullying, threats and sharing intimate images without consent are crimes under the **Cybercrimes Act** (2020). If you are targeted: do not reply, take **screenshots**, **block** and **report** the account, and tell a trusted adult.

notes.label: Digital citizenship
notes.text: A good digital citizen is respectful online, thinks before posting, checks facts before sharing, protects their privacy, stands up against cyberbullying and balances screen time with offline activities.

questions.prompt: When the media expose corruption, they are playing which role?
What is false information that is spread deliberately to deceive people called?
What is the permanent record of your online activity called?
Setting your social media accounts to private helps to protect your safety.
Which South African law makes certain online harms, such as sharing intimate images without consent, a crime?
Match each term to its meaning.

pairs.right: Adult gaining a child's trust to exploit them
Trick to steal money or information

questions.prompt: Describe THREE ways to check whether a news story you see online is true.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): check the author/publisher; check the date; look for evidence; compare with other reliable sources; be wary of emotional headlines; reverse image search

questions.prompt: Give THREE tips for staying safe online.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): don't share personal details; strong passwords; private accounts; don't meet strangers; beware of scams; think before sharing images

questions.prompt: What should you do if you are being cyberbullied?
questions.memo: Any two (1 each): don't reply; take screenshots; block and report; tell a trusted adult; report to police if serious

questions.prompt: Why should teenagers think carefully about their digital footprint?
questions.memo:
